## The question

[Leibniz rule for integrals and symmetry of second derivative](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4662478/leibniz-rule-for-integrals-and-symmetry-of-second-derivative), asked by [Richard Grayson](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/1161679/richard-grayson) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2023-03-20; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> Given two real valued functions $x(t), y(t)$, such that $\dot{y}(t) = \dot{x}(t)$, I need to compute $\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}$. One approach is: 
>
> $$\begin{equation}
> \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial x}(t) = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \int \dot{x} \ dt 
>  = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (x(t) + C) = 1
> \end{equation}$$
>
> On the other hand, using the symmetry of second derivative and taking $F(x,t) = \dot{x}(t)$, it follows that:  
>
> $$\begin{equation} 
> \dfrac{\partial F(x,t)}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial \dot{x}(t)}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial }{\partial x} \dfrac{dx}{dt} = \dfrac{d}{dt} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial x} = \dfrac{d}{dt} 1 = 0
> \end{equation}$$
>
> Therefore, using Leibniz rule for integrals, 
>
> $$\begin{equation}
> \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial x}(t) = \int \dfrac{\partial \dot{x}(t)}{\partial x} \ dt = \int 0 \ dt = C
> \end{equation}$$
>
> With the first approach, we get $\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}$ = 1. With the second, $\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}$ = C $\in \mathbb{R}$. Which of them is correct? Or neither?
:::

It seems to me like you're overthinking it. If $\dot x(t) = \dot y(t)$, then $y(t) = x(t) + C$ for some constant $C$. So $\frac{dy}{dx} = 1$.
